blocks.body:
A smooth complex surface defined by a polynomial equation, such as $x^4 + y^4 + z^4 + w^4 = 0$ in complex projective space, is at the same time three kinds of object: a topological space with holes of various dimensions, a manifold on which one can do calculus with complex coordinates, and an algebraic object built from polynomials. Each viewpoint produces its own invariants. The Hodge conjecture predicts exactly which topological features come from algebra: which "holes" can be filled or traced out by subvarieties cut out by polynomial equations.

This page builds the minimum vocabulary (projective varieties, cohomology, types $(p,q)$), states the conjecture, and explains the cases that are known.

blocks.title: The objects
blocks.body:
Complex projective space $\mathbb{CP}^n$ is the set of nonzero vectors $(z_0, \dots, z_n) \in \mathbb C^{n+1}$ up to scaling by nonzero [[complex-numbers|complex numbers]]. A projective variety $X \subset \mathbb{CP}^n$ is the common zero set of finitely many homogeneous [[polynomials-roots|polynomials]]; it is non-singular if at every point the gradients of the defining polynomials have the expected rank, so that $X$ is a complex manifold. A complex manifold of complex dimension $n$ has real dimension $2n$. A curve ($n = 1$) is a real surface; a non-singular plane cubic curve is topologically a torus.

Inside $X$ we can look for algebraic subvarieties $Z$: subsets of $X$ cut out by further polynomial equations. If $Z$ has complex codimension $p$ in $X$, it has real dimension $2n - 2p$.

blocks.title: Cohomology and the Hodge decomposition
blocks.body:
Cohomology measures holes. The group $H^k(X,\mathbb Q)$ is a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb Q$ whose dimension $b_k$ (the $k$-th Betti number) counts the independent $k$-dimensional holes. For a torus $b_0 = 1$, $b_1 = 2$, $b_2 = 1$. One concrete model: $H^k(X,\mathbb C)$ is the space of closed differential $k$-forms modulo exact ones (de Rham cohomology), and the rational classes $H^k(X,\mathbb Q)$ sit inside it as those whose integrals over all $k$-dimensional cycles with integer coefficients are rational.

In complex coordinates $z_j = x_j + iy_j$ every form is built from $dz_j = dx_j + i\,dy_j$ and $d\bar z_j = dx_j - i\,dy_j$. A form has type $(p,q)$ if each term contains $p$ factors $dz$ and $q$ factors $d\bar z$. Hodge's theorem says that on a non-singular projective variety this splitting passes to cohomology:

$$H^k(X,\mathbb C) = \bigoplus_{p+q=k}H^{p,q}(X), \qquad \overline{H^{p,q}} = H^{q,p}.$$

The Hodge numbers $h^{p,q} = \dim H^{p,q}$ satisfy $b_k = \sum_{p+q=k}h^{p,q}$ and $h^{p,q} = h^{q,p}$. For a curve of genus $g$: $h^{1,0} = h^{0,1} = g$ and $b_1 = 2g$.

blocks.title: Why subvarieties give (p,p) classes
blocks.body:
A subvariety $Z$ of codimension $p$ defines a class $[Z] \in H^{2p}(X,\mathbb Q)$: it is the class that, paired with a closed form $\eta$ of degree $2n-2p$, gives $\int_Z\eta$. Integrals over $Z$ of forms with integer periods are integers, so the class is rational.

It is also of type $(p,p)$. The reason is that $Z$ is itself complex, of complex dimension $m = n - p$. Restricted to $Z$, a form of degree $2m$ can only survive if it has type $(m,m)$: a term with more than $m$ factors $dz$ vanishes on an $m$-dimensional complex manifold, just as $dz_1\wedge dz_1 = 0$. So $\int_Z\eta$ only sees the $(m,m)$ part of $\eta$, and this forces $[Z]$ to lie in $H^{p,p}$. Rational linear combinations of such classes are called algebraic classes.

blocks.title: Hodge classes
blocks.body:
The Hodge classes of degree $2p$ on $X$ are the elements of

$$\operatorname{Hdg}^p(X) = H^{2p}(X,\mathbb Q)\cap H^{p,p}(X).$$

They are the cohomology classes that pass both tests satisfied by algebraic classes: they are rational, and they have type $(p,p)$.

blocks.title: The Hodge conjecture
blocks.body:
Let $X$ be a non-singular complex projective variety. Then every Hodge class is algebraic:

$$H^{2p}(X,\mathbb Q)\cap H^{p,p}(X) = \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q}\{[Z] : Z \subset X \text{ an algebraic subvariety of codimension } p\}.$$

The inclusion $\supseteq$ is the argument above; the conjecture is the inclusion $\subseteq$. Hodge raised the question in 1950.

blocks.title: What is known
blocks.body:
- Lefschetz $(1,1)$ theorem (Lefschetz, 1924; later reproved by Kodaira and Spencer): the conjecture holds for $p = 1$, and even with integer coefficients. Hodge classes in $H^2$ are classes of divisors.
- Using the hard Lefschetz theorem, the case $p = 1$ implies the case $p = n - 1$. Since $p = 0$ and $p = n$ are trivial, the conjecture holds for all varieties of dimension at most $3$. The first open case is $p = 2$ on fourfolds.
- The integral version is false: Atiyah and Hirzebruch (1962) found torsion integral classes that are not algebraic, and Kollár gave non-torsion examples. That is why the conjecture is stated over $\mathbb Q$.
- For general compact Kähler manifolds, which need not be projective, the natural analogue fails (Voisin, 2002).
- Evidence: Cattani, Deligne and Kaplan (1995) proved that the locus where a class stays Hodge, in a family of varieties, is algebraic, which the conjecture predicts. Deligne showed that Hodge classes on abelian varieties are "absolute Hodge", a weaker algebraicity property.

blocks.title: Holomorphic forms vanish on complex curves
blocks.body: In $\mathbb C^2$ with coordinates $(z, w)$, restrict the forms $dz\wedge dw$ (type $(2,0)$) and $dz\wedge d\bar z$ (type $(1,1)$) to the complex line $w = az + b$, parametrised by $z = s + it$ with real $s, t$.
blocks.solution:
On the line, $dw = a\,dz$, so $dz\wedge dw = a\,dz\wedge dz = 0$. In real terms the coefficient of $ds\wedge dt$ is $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial s}\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial t} - \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial t}\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial s} = 1\cdot ai - i\cdot a = 0$.

For $dz\wedge d\bar z$ the coefficient is $1\cdot(-i) - i\cdot 1 = -2i$, so $dz\wedge d\bar z = -2i\,ds\wedge dt$, a nonzero multiple of the area form. Integrals of $(2,0)$ forms over complex curves are always $0$; only the $(1,1)$ part of a $2$-form can be detected by a complex curve. This is the mechanism that puts algebraic classes in $H^{p,p}$.

blocks.title: Curves: the conjecture is easy
blocks.body: A non-singular plane curve of degree $d$ has genus $g = (d-1)(d-2)/2$. Compute $g$ for $d = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ and explain why the Hodge conjecture is trivially true for curves.
blocks.solution:
The genera are $0, 0, 1, 3, 6$. So lines and conics are spheres, cubics are tori, and quartics have three handles.

For a curve ($n = 1$) the only possible $p$ are $0$ and $1$. $H^0$ is spanned by the class of the whole curve, and $H^2(X,\mathbb Q)$ is one-dimensional, spanned by the class of a point (a codimension $1$ subvariety). Both are algebraic, so every Hodge class is algebraic. The interesting middle group $H^1$ has odd degree and contains no Hodge classes at all.

blocks.title: Hodge numbers of surfaces in projective 3-space
blocks.body: For a non-singular surface of degree $d$ in $\mathbb{CP}^3$ one has $b_1 = 0$, Euler characteristic $\chi = d^3 - 4d^2 + 6d$, and $h^{2,0} = \binom{d-1}{3}$. Compute $b_2$, $h^{2,0}$ and $h^{1,1}$ for $d = 4$ and $d = 5$, and check $d = 1, 2$ against known spaces.
blocks.solution:
Since $b_0 = b_4 = 1$ and $b_1 = b_3 = 0$, $b_2 = \chi - 2 = d^3 - 4d^2 + 6d - 2$, and $h^{1,1} = b_2 - 2h^{2,0}$.

- $d = 1$: $\chi = 3$, the Euler characteristic of the projective plane. $d = 2$: $\chi = 4$, that of $\mathbb{CP}^1\times\mathbb{CP}^1$, which is what a smooth quadric is.
- $d = 4$ (a K3 surface): $b_2 = 22$, $h^{2,0} = 1$, $h^{1,1} = 20$.
- $d = 5$: $b_2 = 53$, $h^{2,0} = 4$, $h^{1,1} = 45$.

For a quartic surface, which classes in the $22$-dimensional $H^2(X,\mathbb Q)$ are Hodge depends delicately on the coefficients of the equation: the rational classes lying in the $20$-dimensional subspace $H^{1,1}$ form a space whose dimension (the Picard number) depends on the equation and always lies between $1$ and $20$. Lefschetz's theorem guarantees that all of them are classes of curves on the surface. The conjecture asks for the same phenomenon in higher codimension, where no analogue of Lefschetz's proof is known.

blocks.body:
- Both conditions matter. Classes of type $(p,p)$ with complex coefficients are far more numerous; the conjecture concerns rational classes of type $(p,p)$.
- The integral Hodge conjecture is false; use $\mathbb Q$.
- Non-singular and projective are essential hypotheses; the analogue for general compact Kähler manifolds fails.
- Known low-dimensional cases come from $p = 1$; they do not suggest a method for $p = 2$.

The conjecture lives where [[complex-numbers|complex analysis]] ([[holomorphic]]) meets the algebra of [[polynomials-roots|polynomial equations]] and topology. Its arithmetic cousins, the Tate conjecture and the conjectures on algebraic cycles, connect with [[bsd]] and with the zeta functions of varieties over [[finite-fields]]. It is one of the Millennium problems with [[rh]], [[p-vs-np]], [[navier-stokes]], [[yang-mills]], [[bsd]] and the solved [[poincare]].

1. Show that a form of type $(2,0)$ on $\mathbb C^2$ restricts to zero on every complex line.
2. Verify $b_2 = 22$ for the quartic surface from the Euler characteristic formula, and explain why $h^{2,0} = h^{0,2}$.
3. Why can odd-degree cohomology contain no Hodge classes?
4. Compute $h^{1,1}$ for a non-singular surface of degree $6$ in $\mathbb{CP}^3$.
